metadata.title: Examining key capitals contributing to students' science-related career expectations and their relationship patterns: A machine learning approach
metadata.venue: Journal of Research in Science Teaching

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata (519,334 students aged 15) and constructs a binary outcome from students’ reported science-related career expectations (ISCO-coded job expectations). The manuscript describes PISA’s use of IRT to estimate latent traits and that PISA provides 10 plausible values for academic achievement domains, but it does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the random forest estimation. Because the model is a Random Forest classifier trained in R after KNN imputation and feature standardization, the authors do not specify any complex-survey-weight adjustment; thus, analysts should treat the results as model-based prediction rather than fully design-weighted population estimates. For replication, users should consult the PISA 2015 technical documentation for the appropriate student weight variables and replicate-weight scheme, and then decide whether to incorporate them via a survey-aware ML workflow (not described here).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 (science major domain) for 15-year-old students from 72 countries/economies. Outcome coding: students’ expected job at age ~30 (ST114/OCOD3) recoded to a binary science-related career expectation (1=science/ICT/health/science technicians; 0=otherwise). Analytic sample restrictions for global model: deleted students who did not report career aspirations (n=65,146) and deleted students with missing values over half of the selected contextual features (n=40,252), dropping 105,398 students total (missing-case rate 20.29%). Remaining missing values in contextual features were imputed using KNN; features were standardized before imputation and then de-standardized prior to Random Forest training. Regional analysis was conducted separately for Hong Kong using the same procedure; the paper does not report additional Hong Kong-specific filtering beyond the shared steps.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Number of science classes per week

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) — global model (science-related career expectations; binary)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (top 25 features): 10-fold CV average AUC=0.7959, sensitivity=0.7106, specificity=0.7324. Test set: AUC=0.7419, sensitivity=0.6655, specificity=0.6893, accuracy=0.6818 (95% CI [0.6786, 0.6850]). Unseen complete-sample test: AUC=0.7463, sensitivity=0.6836, specificity=0.6772, accuracy=0.6816 (95% CI [0.6784, 0.6847]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) global model the study leveraged instrumental motivation (science), parents’ expectations for a science career, enjoyment of science, science performance, and teacher fairness to predict science-related career expectation (binary), finding that the Random Forest achieved decent discrimination (test AUC=0.7419) and that key science-capital factors were among the most important predictors. This indicates that strengthening malleable science-capital resources—especially students’ motivational dispositions and parents’ science expectations—may improve students’ science-related career aspirations, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) — Hong Kong regional model (science-related career expectations; binary)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (top 10 features): 10-fold CV average AUC=0.9190, sensitivity=0.8052, specificity=0.8458. Test set: AUC=0.7660, sensitivity=0.7008, specificity=0.7056, accuracy=0.7044 (95% CI [0.6744, 0.7330]). Unseen complete-sample test: AUC=0.7685, sensitivity=0.7031, specificity=0.7051, accuracy=0.7045 (95% CI [0.6742, 0.7336]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Hong Kong regional model the study leveraged instrumental motivation (science), parents’ expectations for a science career, enjoyment of science, science performance, and parental current support at home to predict science-related career expectation (binary), finding that the Random Forest showed strong cross-validated discrimination (10-fold CV AUC=0.9190) and stable test performance (test AUC≈0.766–0.769). This indicates that while many globally important science-capital factors generalize to Hong Kong, some social-capital features (e.g., parental support characteristics) may be context-specific for tailoring interventions.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 519,334 15-year-old students from 72 countries/economies, predicting a binary indicator of science-related career expectations (science/ICT/health/science technician occupations vs other jobs). A Random Forest classifier was trained after deleting students who did not report career aspirations and those with missingness in more than half of selected contextual features, then imputing remaining missing contextual variables via KNN; features were standardized prior to imputation. For achievement-related predictors, the authors used PISA’s 10 plausible values by repeating analyses across all 10 PVs and aggregating results. In the global model (top 25 features), performance was AUC=0.7419 with test accuracy=0.6818; in Hong Kong (top 10 features), test AUC was about 0.766–0.769. The paper uses ALE plots for relationship-shape interpretation (increasing, S-shaped, inverted-U, decreasing) but, because PISA is cross-sectional, the findings support predictive importance and associations rather than causal effects.
